LONDON, England (CNN)  -- Charging chesty women more for their bras doesn't win a lot of support, British retailer Marks & Spencer acknowledged Friday as it announced an end to the surcharge on its larger lingerie. Marks & Spencer have apologised for charging chesty women more for bras. "We boobed," screamed a full-page Marks & Spencer ad, which appeared in British newspapers Friday. Marks & Spencer gave in to campaigners who argued that the higher prices of the bigger bras was unfair. The retailer charged as much as £2 ($3) more for all sizes DD and up. "It's true that our fantastic quality larger bras cost more money to make, and we felt it was right to reflect this in the prices we charged," the ad said. "Well, we were wrong." It follows a nearly year-long campaign by members of the Facebook group Busts 4 Justice. The women behind the site argued other chain retailers didn't charge extra for bigger sizes, so Marks & Spencer shouldn't, either. And it pointed out that the store doesn't charge extra for larger sizes of clothing, so it shouldn't charge more for larger undergarments. What's your view? "We would like to thank everyone who has supported us on this issue; especially the thousands of brilliant, busty women that have joined forces with us. We couldn't have done this without you," the two administrators of the group, Becky Mount and Beckie Williams, posted Friday on Facebook. "Busts 4 Justice remain committed to making things better for busty women on the high street, but for now we're happy just to be able to encourage all ladies to reward themselves and their boobs with some properly fitted, fairly priced lingerie." Marks & Spencer is a stalwart British chain, known for classic wardrobe staples and low prices. Its underwear department is the first stop for many British shoppers and is especially famous for reliable basics. And to give customers an added lift, Marks & Spencer also announced it is cutting the prices of all of its bras by 25 percent for the rest of May. "I think even though we all obviously held a bit of a grudge against buying our bras from M&S we should really be grateful they got rid of the surcharge and have given us the super generous 25 percent off," Mount wrote on the group's site Friday. "They may get cleared out by the time the weekend is over!"

**Victory for ‘Busts 4 Justice’: How a Grassroots Campaign Forced Marks & Spencer to Scrap Its Controversial Lingerie Tax**

In a landmark triumph for consumer activism, British retail giant Marks & Spencer (M&S) capitulated to overwhelming public pressure by abandoning its controversial pricing policy on women’s lingerie. The move came after a year-long, highly publicized campaign spearheaded by a Facebook group known as "Busts 4 Justice," which rallied thousands of women against what had become widely dubbed the "bust tax."

For years, Marks & Spencer—traditionally the UK’s market leader in bras and lingerie—maintained a policy of charging up to £2 more for bras in size DD and above. The retailer justified the price discrepancy by citing the additional engineering, fabric, and manufacturing costs required to produce larger, more supportive garments. 

However, female consumers viewed the surcharge as inherently unfair and discriminatory. Critics pointed out a stark double standard in the retailer's pricing strategy: M&S did not charge extra for larger sizes in men’s clothing, such as waistcoats or extra-large T-shirts, despite those items requiring additional fabric. 

The turning point began when 26-year-old consumer Beckie Williams, frustrated by paying more for her bra size, decided to take action. She launched the "Busts 4 Justice" campaign on Facebook. What started as a localized grievance quickly struck a chord with women across the United Kingdom. Utilizing the emerging power of social media, the group grew rapidly, transforming online complaints into a coordinated national movement. Members organized boycotts, engaged with national media outlets, and even bought single shares in Marks & Spencer to attend the company’s annual general meeting and confront executives directly.

Initially, M&S leadership held its ground, defending the cost breakdown of manufacturing larger intimate wear. But as media coverage intensified and consumer outrage threatened to damage the brand’s carefully cultivated reputation as a trusted, high-street institution, the company’s stance became untenable. 

Conceding defeat, M&S Chief Executive Sir Stuart Rose issued a full, public apology to customers. Admitting that the company had misjudged public sentiment, Rose acknowledged that M&S should have absorbed the additional manufacturing costs rather than passing them on to women with larger busts.

To make amends, M&S announced a series of decisive steps:
* **Immediate Removal of the Surcharge:** Effective immediately, bras of all sizes were set to the same base price, permanently ending the £2 extra fee for DD+ sizes.
* **A Store-Wide Price Cut:** In an unprecedented gesture of goodwill, M&S launched a national promotion cutting the price of *all* bras across its stores by 25 percent.
* **A Commitment to Equal Pricing:** The retailer pledged that moving forward, price parity across all sizing tiers would remain a permanent policy.

The resolution was celebrated as a historic victory for consumer power in the digital age. By leveraging social media, "Busts 4 Justice" demonstrated that ordinary shoppers could successfully hold corporate titans accountable. Beyond the immediate financial relief for millions of women, the campaign set a lasting precedent for fair pricing standards across the retail industry, sending a clear message that consumers would no longer tolerate unfair surcharges based on body shape or size.

**LONDON (CNN)** — In a major victory for consumer power, British retail giant Marks & Spencer has announced a dramatic U-turn, scrapping its controversial price surcharge on larger bra sizes following a fierce, nation-wide campaign by shoppers.

The high-street titan—which sells more than one-third of all bras in the United Kingdom—had drawn the ire of women across the country for charging up to £2 ($3 USD) more for bras in cup sizes DD and above, a practice dubbed by critics as a discriminatory "tax on larger breasts."

On Friday, M&S conceded defeat, taking out full-page advertisements in national newspapers with a blunt, four-word headline: **“We got it wrong.”**

Starting immediately, the retailer announced that all bras will cost the same price, regardless of cup size.

### A victory for 'Busts 4 Justice'

The corporate retreat comes after months of mounting pressure led by 26-year-old customer Becky Williams. Frustrated by paying extra for her size-G bras, Williams launched a grassroots online campaign called "Busts 4 Justice," which quickly mobilized tens of thousands of supporters.

The movement gained global attention and took a dramatic turn when activists bought shares in Marks & Spencer, planning to confront board members directly at the company's annual general meeting.

"It felt like we were being penalized for something we have no control over," Williams said following the announcement. "You don't choose your bra size. Today proves that when consumers stand together, even the biggest corporations have to listen."

### The engineering defense falls flat

Marks & Spencer had initially defended the tiered pricing structure, arguing that larger bras require more fabric, specialized design, and extra structural support. Executives maintained that the £2 surcharge merely reflected higher manufacturing costs.

However, critics were quick to point out that M&S did not charge extra for larger men’s suits or women’s dresses, making the bra surcharge appear uniquely unfair.

In a statement, M&S Executive Chairman Sir Stuart Rose admitted the company had misjudged the mood of its customer base.

"We saw it as a feature of the manufacturing costs, but our customers saw it as a tax on larger sizes," Rose said. "We heard them loud and clear. Moving forward, a bra will cost the same whether you're an A-cup or a GG."

To prove its point, M&S announced it will also run a promotional discount across all bra sizes to make amends with customers.

### A warning shot to retailers

Industry analysts say the capitulation by M&S serves as a stark warning to brands about the growing power of organized consumer campaigns in the digital age.

"M&S is a British institution, but they completely misread the room," said Amanda Johnston, a retail analyst at London-based firm Retail Economics. "In today’s market, perception is everything. Trying to justify a price hike on a basic necessity based on body size was never going to win in the court of public opinion."

For Williams and the thousands of women who joined her campaign, the mood today is celebratory—a sign that high-street giants can no longer ignore the voices of the people who keep them in business.

counterfactuals.prompt: What happened with the Marks & Spencer "Busts 4 Justice" campaign over bra pricing?
counterfactuals.output:
The **"Busts 4 Justice"** campaign was a high-profile consumer boycott and PR crisis for the British retailer Marks & Spencer (M&S) in **2009**. It centered on M&S’s practice of charging more for larger-sized bras—a surcharge that critics dubbed a "tax on big boobs."

Here is the story of how the campaign unfolded, how M&S initially defended itself, and the dramatic public policy U-turn that followed.

---

### 1. The Controversy: The "Surcharge on Big Bras"
In early 2009, M&S—which was the UK's market leader in lingerie, holding around a 20% market share—was charging **£2 more** for bras in DD-cup sizes and larger compared to the exact same style in A–D cups. 

For example, a bra that cost £14 in a size 34B cost £16 in a size 34DD. 

### 2. The Campaign Begins
The issue gained widespread attention when **Beckie Williams**, a 26-year-old customer from Oxfordshire who wore a DD+ cup, noticed the price discrepancy. Feeling that women were being financially penalized for their natural body shapes, she launched a Facebook group called **"Busts 4 Justice."**

The campaign quickly went viral, attracting over 14,000 members in a matter of weeks. Women expressed outrage, arguing:
* It was discriminatory toward women with larger busts.
* Clothing for larger men or taller people was rarely marked up in the same explicit way.
* M&S was essentially imposing a "breast tax."

### 3. M&S’s Initial Defense
At first, M&S stood its ground. Executive Chairman **Sir Stuart Rose** and M&S management defended the price gap, citing legitimate manufacturing costs:
* **Engineering and Materials:** They argued that larger bras required significantly more fabric, specialized structural support, stronger underwires, and thicker straps.
* **Cost Allocation:** M&S claimed that forcing smaller-busted women to pay a single flat price would mean they were unfairly "subsidizing" the higher production costs of larger bras.

### 4. Escalation and the Shareholder Meeting
The campaign escalated when Beckie Williams bought a single share in Marks & Spencer so she could legally attend the company's Annual General Meeting (AGM) to confront the board directly. 

The story was picked up by national newspapers, TV news, and talk shows. The bad publicity began to severely damage M&S’s image as a consumer-friendly brand that supported women.

### 5. The U-Turn: "We Boofed"
Realizing they were losing the public relations battle, M&S completely backed down in **May 2009**. 

Sir Stuart Rose publicly apologized, acknowledging that the company had misjudged the mood of its customer base. M&S announced that:
1. **Equal Pricing:** All bras, regardless of size, would cost the same going forward.
2. **Price Reductions:** The prices of all larger bras were reduced by £2 to match the smaller sizes (rather than raising the price of smaller bras).
3. **PR Campaign:** M&S launched a cheeky full-page national newspaper ad campaign admitting their mistake. The ad featured a model in a bra with the headline: **"We boofed"** (a play on "goofed" and "boobs").
4. **Peace Offering:** M&S offered a 25% discount on all bras for a limited time to win back customer goodwill.

### Significance and Legacy
The "Busts 4 Justice" campaign became a landmark case study in modern retail PR and consumer power. It demonstrated:
* **The Power of Social Media:** It was one of the earliest UK examples of a Facebook group forcing a major FTSE 100 corporation into an immediate operational U-turn.
* **Pricing Perception vs. Cost:** It showed that even if a business has a logical supply-chain justification for a price difference (higher material costs), consumer perception of fairness often trumps pure cost-plus pricing logic.

**The Price of Fit: How a Viral Campaign Forced a Fashion Giant to Drop Its ‘Plus-Size Tax’**

*After weeks of digital boycotts and viral receipts, Verve Intimates capitulated to consumer outrage, standardizing prices across all sizing options.*

**NEW YORK** — It started with a six-dollar discrepancy on a digital receipt. It ended with a multi-million-dollar policy shift for one of the nation’s largest innerwear brands.

On Tuesday, digital-first lingerie giant Verve Intimates announced it would immediately standardize pricing across its entire product line, officially ending a controversial tiered-pricing model that charged customers up to 20% more for sizes XL and above. 

The reversal comes after a grueling, three-week online campaign led by a coalition of body-positivity advocates, micro-influencers, and everyday shoppers who successfully framed the pricing model not as a business necessity, but as a discriminatory "plus-size tax."

### The Six-Dollar Difference

The controversy erupted in late October when Maya Lin, a 28-year-old digital strategist from Chicago, posted a 45-second TikTok video showing her online shopping cart at Verve. Her video highlighted two identical lace bralettes in the same color: the size Small was listed at $32, while the 2XL was priced at $38.

“We’re told that fashion is becoming more inclusive, but apparently inclusivity comes with a surcharge,” Lin said in the video, which quickly amassed over 4 million views. “If a brand doesn’t discount an Extra-Small for using less fabric, why are they penalizing larger bodies for using more?”

Within days, the hashtag **#PayTheSame** began trending across TikTok, Instagram, and X (formerly Twitter). Shoppers flooded Verve’s comment sections with screenshots of similar price disparities across their catalog, from everyday cotton briefs to high-end shapewear. 

The backlash quickly transformed into a coordinated movement. An online petition demanding price parity gathered more than 150,000 signatures in less than a week, and influencers with hundreds of thousands of followers publicly canceled their affiliate contracts with the brand.

### The Material Argument vs. The Consumer Reality

In the initial days of the controversy, Verve sought to defend its pricing structure. In a now-deleted statement released last week, the company cited the economic realities of garment manufacturing.

"Producing extended sizes requires additional raw materials, specialized grading, and re-engineered support structures to ensure proper fit," a company spokesperson stated at the time. "Our pricing reflects the true cost of production for each individual garment."

Historically, the apparel industry has relied on this defense. Manufacturing garments in larger sizes often requires distinct patterns, additional fabric, and different machinery calibration. 

However, retail analysts note that this argument has become increasingly difficult to defend in the court of public opinion, particularly in an era where brand values drive purchasing decisions.

“From a pure supply chain perspective, extra fabric and unique grading do cost more,” said Sarah Jenkins, a senior retail analyst at Lumina Commerce. “But from a brand equity perspective, isolating your plus-size consumer base is disastrous. Brands routinely absorb margins on lower-volume items—like specialized colors or intricate trims—without passing that cost directly to the consumer. Singling out size felt punitive to shoppers.”

Critics were also quick to point out that Verve’s pricing model was asymmetrical: smaller sizes (XS and XXS), which use significantly less material than a Medium or Large, carried no discount.

### A Rapid Capitulation

As calls for a holiday-season boycott grew louder and Verve’s app store rating plunged from 4.8 to 1.8 stars overnight, the company’s executive leadership folded.

In a video statement released Tuesday morning, Verve CEO Elena Rostova announced a complete overhaul of the company's pricing strategy.

"We listened, and we got it wrong," Rostova said. "Fashion should empower, not create barriers. Effective immediately, every garment at Verve will carry the exact same price tag, regardless of size. To those we alienated: we hear you, and we are committed to doing better."

In addition to unifying prices, Verve announced it would issue automatic store credits to any customer who had purchased an extended-size item at the higher price point over the past six months—an olive branch estimated to cost the retailer upwards of $2.5 million.

### A Precedent for the Industry

The victory at Verve is being hailed by consumer advocates as a watershed moment for size equity in fashion. While a handful of major retailers, such as Target and Old Navy, moved to standardized pricing in recent years, many mid-tier and luxury intimate brands still charge premiums for extended sizing.

For Maya Lin, the woman whose TikTok sparked the movement, the outcome proves the power of collective consumer action in the digital age.

“This wasn’t just about six dollars,” Lin told reporters on Tuesday. “It was about the principle that women shouldn’t be financially penalized for the body shape they have. Today showed that when consumers stand together, brands have no choice but to listen.”

Industry experts predict that Verve’s retreat will send shockwaves through the retail sector, likely prompting competitor brands to quietly audit their own pricing structures before they become the next target of a viral campaign.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
